title: Divergence and curl
objectives: Compute the divergence and curl of a field and read what they measure.

screens.title: Dye and paddle wheels
screens.prose: Picture each field as a flowing liquid. Put a drop of dye in the small square: does it spread out? Put a tiny paddle wheel there: does it spin? Flip through pictures A to C.
screens.question: Answer yes or no for each picture.

hints.text: Watch the arrows on the four corners of the square.
In C the arrows on opposite sides point away from each other.
A turns everything round the origin; B moves the square without changing it; C pushes it apart.

feedback.correct: A spins without spreading, B does neither, C spreads without spinning.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the arrows on opposite sides of the square.

explain.text: In C the far side moves out faster than the near side, so the dye spreads. In A the square turns as it moves, so a wheel spins. In B every point moves the same way: nothing spreads or turns.

screens.title: Two numbers for each field
screens.prose: The **divergence** $\nabla \cdot \mathbf F = P_x + Q_y$ measures spreading. The scalar **curl** $\operatorname{curl}\mathbf F = Q_x - P_y$ measures spin, counterclockwise positive. The picture is the shear $(y, 0)$.
screens.question: Fill in both numbers for each field.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the four partials of each field.

byKey.sign: The curl is $Q_x - P_y = 0 - 1 = -1$, not $P_y - Q_x$.

explain.text: Outward spreads at rate 2 and rotation spins at rate 2. The shear spins at $-1$; the uniform field does neither. The trap screen explains the shear's spin.

screens.title: Why $P_x + Q_y$ measures spreading
screens.prose: Take a small square of side $h$ centred at $(x, y)$. The flow out through a side is the outward part of $\mathbf F$ times the side's length. Arrange the argument.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: Out through the right and left sides: $\left[P(x + \tfrac h2, y) - P(x - \tfrac h2, y)\right]h$. (Outward part times length.)
$\approx P_x h \cdot h = P_x h^2$. (Linear approximation, as in Multivariable Calculus.)
Top and bottom give $\left[Q(x, y + \tfrac h2) - Q(x, y - \tfrac h2)\right]h \approx Q_y h^2$. (The same steps in $y$.)
Divide the total $(P_x + Q_y)h^2$ by the area $h^2$. (Outflow per unit area.)
Let $h \to 0$: the outflow per unit area is $P_x + Q_y$. (The approximation becomes exact.)
Out through the right and left sides: $\left[Q(x + \tfrac h2, y) - Q(x - \tfrac h2, y)\right]h$. (Outward part.)
lines.why: On a vertical side the outward direction is along $x$, so $P$ crosses it, not $Q$.

hints.text: Start with the flow through the vertical sides.

feedback.correct: Divergence is outflow per unit area as the square shrinks.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each line needs the one before it.

byKey.d1: You used $Q$ on the vertical sides. $Q$ runs along them; $P$ crosses them.

explain.text: The two vertical sides net $P_x h^2$ and the two horizontal sides $Q_y h^2$. Per unit area that is $P_x + Q_y$, exact as $h \to 0$ for $\mathbf F$ with continuous partials.

screens.title: Divergence of a new field
screens.prose: Take $\mathbf F = (x^2y,\ x - y^2)$. The heat map behind the arrows shades $P_x + Q_y$.
screens.question: Find $\nabla \cdot \mathbf F$.

byKey.curl: That is the curl, $Q_x - P_y$. Divergence takes $P_x + Q_y$.

explain.text: $P_x = 2xy$ and $Q_y = -2y$, so $\nabla \cdot \mathbf F = 2xy - 2y$. It is 0 along $y = 0$ and along $x = 1$.

screens.title: Curl of the same field
screens.prose: Same field, $\mathbf F = (x^2y,\ x - y^2)$. Now the heat map shades $Q_x - P_y$.
screens.question: Find $\operatorname{curl}\mathbf F = Q_x - P_y$.

byKey.swap: You took $P_y - Q_x$. The curl is $Q_x - P_y$.
byKey.div: That is the divergence. Curl takes $Q_x - P_y$.

explain.text: $Q_x = 1$ and $P_y = x^2$. So the spin is counterclockwise for $|x| < 1$ and clockwise beyond.

screens.title: At one point
screens.prose: Divergence and curl are numbers at each point. Evaluate both at $(2, 1)$.
screens.question: Fill in both values at $(2, 1)$.

feedback.correct: Divergence 2 and curl $-3$: spreading, with a clockwise spin.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Substitute into both formulas.

explain.text: At $(2, 1)$ the flow spreads at rate 2 and spins clockwise at rate 3. Signs matter: a negative curl turns clockwise.

screens.title: Curl in space
screens.prose: In space $\nabla \cdot \mathbf F = P_x + Q_y + R_z$, and the curl is a vector, $\nabla \times \mathbf F = (R_y - Q_z,\ P_z - R_x,\ Q_x - P_y)$. Each entry is a planar curl in the plane at right angles to one axis. Take $\mathbf F = (xy,\ yz,\ zx)$.
screens.question: What is $\nabla \times \mathbf F$ at $(1, 2, 3)$? Give $(a, b, c)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the six partials one entry at a time.

byKey.sign: Each entry is a difference in a fixed order: $R_y - Q_z = 0 - y$.
byKey.length: Give three entries, one per axis.

explain.text: $R_y - Q_z = -y$, $P_z - R_x = -z$ and $Q_x - P_y = -x$. At $(1, 2, 3)$ that is $(-2, -3, -1)$, and the divergence is $y + z + x = 6$.

screens.title: Two identities
screens.prose:
For $f$ with continuous second partials, $\operatorname{curl}
abla f = f_{yx} - f_{xy} = 0$ by Clairaut. And $
abla \cdot 
abla f = f_{xx} + f_{yy}$ is the **Laplacian**, the operator in the heat equation of the PDEs course.
screens.question: Fill in the Laplacian of each function.

hints.text: Differentiate each twice in $x$, then twice in $y$.

byKey.abs: $f_{yy} = -2$ for $x^2 - y^2$, so the sum is 0.

explain.text: $\nabla(x^2 + y^2) = (2x, 2y)$ spreads at rate 4. The gradient of $x^2 - y^2$, drawn here, spreads at rate 0: it is a saddle's flow.

screens.title: Parallel arrows can still spin
screens.prose: The shear $(y, 0)$ has every arrow horizontal. Its curl is $-1$. Picture a paddle wheel centred at $(1.6, 1)$.
screens.question: Does the paddle wheel spin?

options.text: Yes, clockwise: the top is pushed harder than the bottom
No: the arrows are parallel, so nothing turns
options.why: You read spin from the arrows' directions. Spin comes from how the push changes across the wheel.

canvas.caption: The top of the wheel is pushed harder than the bottom, so it turns clockwise.

options.why: A negative curl turns clockwise. The faster top pushes the wheel rightward over the top.

options.text: Only on the $x$-axis, where the arrows vanish
options.why: On the $x$-axis the push is 0 at the centre but not across the wheel: the curl is $-1$ everywhere.

hints.text: Compare the arrows above and below the wheel's centre.
Higher up, $y$ is bigger, so the push is stronger.
Stronger on top, weaker below: a clockwise turn.

feedback.correct: Clockwise, at the rate the curl $-1$ gives.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the push on the top and bottom of the wheel.

byKey.par: You took parallel arrows to mean no spin. The push grows with height, so the wheel's top goes faster: it turns clockwise.

explain.text: $\operatorname{curl}(y, 0) = 0 - 1 = -1$ at every point. The push grows with $y$, so the top of any wheel goes faster than the bottom. Parallel arrows of unequal length can still turn a wheel.

canvas.caption: The top of the wheel is pushed harder than the bottom, so it turns clockwise.

screens.title: A source with a hole
screens.prose: The source field $\mathbf F = \dfrac{(x, y)}{x^2 + y^2}$ points outwards with length $\tfrac1r$. Away from the origin, $P_x + Q_y = \dfrac{y^2 - x^2}{(x^2 + y^2)^2} + \dfrac{x^2 - y^2}{(x^2 + y^2)^2}$.
screens.question: Where is the divergence 0?

options.text: At every point except the origin, where the field is undefined

options.why: At the origin the formula divides by 0, so the divergence does not exist there.

options.text: Nowhere: arrows point outwards, so it spreads
options.why: The arrows shrink like $\tfrac1r$ as they spread, and the two effects cancel exactly.
The two terms cancel at every point off the origin, not only on the axes.

hints.text: That holds wherever the bottom is non-zero.

feedback.correct: Divergence 0 off the origin; undefined at it. Lesson 8 returns to this field.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the two terms.

explain.text: The terms cancel at every point off the origin. The arrows spread out but weaken like $\tfrac1r$, so no small square gains or loses. The origin is a hole that lesson 8 measures.

screens.title: A rates model's drift
screens.prose: Two rate factors $x$ and $y$ revert to their long-run level at the origin. The drift is $\boldsymbol\mu = (-0.5x - 0.3y,\ 0.3x - 0.5y)$. Divergence says whether paths crowd together; curl whether they turn.
screens.question: Fill in $\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol\mu$ and $\operatorname{curl}\boldsymbol\mu$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the four partials.

explain.text: Negative divergence means paths crowd together towards the long-run level. Positive curl means they turn counterclockwise as they do.

screens.title: Pick the phase picture
screens.prose: Flip through four drift fields and drag the start $S$ to see each path. Which picture has divergence $-1$ and curl 0.6?
screens.question: Which picture is this model's drift?

options.why: A has curl $-0.6$: it turns the other way.
B has divergence $-1$ but curl 0, so paths do not turn.
D has divergence $+1$: paths spread away from the long-run level.

hints.text: Find the inward spiral that turns counterclockwise.

feedback.correct: C: the paths spiral in counterclockwise to the long-run level.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the sign of each number.

explain.text: Picture C is $\boldsymbol\mu$ itself. Its matrix has eigenvalues $-0.5 \pm 0.3i$: the inward spiral of the Differential Equations course's phase planes.

ideas: Divergence $P_x + Q_y$ is the outflow per unit area at a point; negative divergence crowds paths together.
The scalar curl $Q_x - P_y$ is the spin at a point, counterclockwise positive; parallel arrows of unequal length can spin.

For $f$ with continuous second partials, $\operatorname{curl}
abla f = 0$, and $
abla \cdot 
abla f$ is the Laplacian.

formula.name: Divergence and curl
formula.tex: \nabla \cdot \mathbf F = P_x + Q_y, \quad \operatorname{curl}\mathbf F = Q_x - P_y
formula.note: In space the curl is the vector (R_y − Q_z, P_z − R_x, Q_x − P_y).

summary.trap: Saying the shear $(y, 0)$ does not spin because its arrows are parallel.

byKey.curl-sum: You added the curl's entries. Divergence adds $P_x + Q_y + R_z$.

explain.text: $P_x = y$, $Q_y = z$ and $R_z = x$, so the divergence at $(1, 2, 3)$ is $2 + 3 + 1 = 6$.

quiz.question: For $f$ with continuous second partials, what is $\operatorname{curl}\nabla f$?

options.why: That is the divergence of $\nabla f$, the Laplacian.
The curl of a field in the plane is a number, not a vector.
It is 0 for every such $f$: $f_{yx} - f_{xy} = 0$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write $Q_x - P_y$ with $P = f_x$, $Q = f_y$.

explain.text: With $P = f_x$ and $Q = f_y$, the curl is $f_{yx} - f_{xy}$. Clairaut makes it 0.

quiz.question: What are the divergence and curl of $\mathbf F = (y, x)$? Give $(\text{div}, \text{curl})$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. $P = y$ and $Q = x$.

byKey.rot: That is $(-y, x)$. For $(y, x)$, $Q_x - P_y = 1 - 1 = 0$.
byKey.length: Give two numbers: divergence, then curl.

explain.text: $P_x + Q_y = 0 + 0$ and $Q_x - P_y = 1 - 1$. The field is $\nabla(xy)$, so its curl must be 0.

quiz.question: What is the Laplacian of $f = x^3 - 3xy^2$?

explain.text: $f_{xx} = 6x$ and $f_{yy} = -6x$, so the Laplacian is 0 everywhere. Such an $f$ is called harmonic.
